ch04.card: Part 3 of 10. The thinker: rounds of looking and passing notes.
ch04.s01.c1: What does a small mind do with a hard question? This is the thinker, the second part of the model. It does the thinking.
ch04.s01.c2: It is ours. It starts from scratch and learns only from our practice.
ch04.s01.c3: The planned size is about 100 million numbers. That size has never been tested.
ch04.s02.c1: Picture only. Imagine a small team of note-takers around one question.
ch04.s02.c2: Each round, every note-taker looks at the whole question again.
ch04.s02.c3: Then they pass notes to each other, and write down what they now believe.
ch04.s02.c4: Same team, same habits, lap after lap.
ch04.s03.c1: A vector is a list of numbers, like a note card with a row of numbers. Letters and notes are vectors.
ch04.s03.c2: It keeps 8 control vectors. Two of them steer the work.
ch04.s03.c3: How many note cards? 36 memory vectors, where its notes are kept.
ch04.s03.c4: Older builds had 17 vectors: 8 control and 9 memory.
ch04.s04.c1: In the tested version, after each round from round 2 on, the call writer reads control vector 0.
ch04.s04.c2: It writes a slip for the outside calculator, like sub 12, 5, or nothing. The calculator is plain code, not AI.
ch04.s04.c3: The numbers on the slip are usually copied from the question or an earlier reply.
ch04.s05.c1: Controls 2 to 7 feed no output. They only pass information along when the notes look at each other. Can we switch them off?
ch04.s05.c2: In an older build, switching them off at test time cost 1.6 points on the main test. Scores are points out of 100.
ch04.s05.c3: On the multi-step test, it hurt far more. They cost 7.8 points: 99.4 fell to 91.6.
ch04.s05.c4: Those numbers are one copy, seed 200. All six copies of that older design lost points, very unevenly.
ch04.s06.c1: Step 1: look. Each letter of the question is one box. A borrowed reader, Gemma, has already given each letter its meaning.
ch04.s06.c2: Each note looks at every letter. In the new design, it also looks at replies the whole reader has read.
ch04.s06.c3: The shading inside each note is a picture only, not real numbers.
ch04.s07.c1: Step 2: the notes talk to each other. In code this is called self-attention.
ch04.s07.c2: Each note reads the other notes and keeps what matters from them.
ch04.s07.c3: The letters are not compared with each other inside the thinker.
ch04.s07.c4: Step 3: each note goes through a small network, the thinking step.
ch04.s07.c5: At the 100M step, it widens to 4.8 times as many numbers, then squeezes back.
ch04.s07.c6: Then the notes go on to the next round.
ch04.s08.c1: One look, compare and think unit is a block. The same blocks run in every round.
ch04.s08.c2: The learned numbers are the same each round. Same team, same habits.
ch04.s08.c3: A round stamp, a learned tag for the round number, is added each round. The older design ran this way.
ch04.s09.c1: Tested design, traced only. Tom has 12 apples, gives away 5, then buys 3. After round 2, the call writer writes sub 12, 5.
ch04.s09.c2: It copies 12 and 5. The outside calculator replies 7. The reader reads it, and adds it to the notes.
ch04.s09.c3: Round 3 sees that reply. Then the call writer writes add 7, 3, and the calculator replies 10.
ch04.s09.c4: Today's stand-in talker copies 10; the planned one has no pointer. New design: the talker writes calls, and replies start the next turn.
ch04.s10.c1: How does it know when to stop? A tiny learned stop switch, the bell, asks: is this settled, or should it think more?
ch04.s10.c2: It must think at least 1 round. It can never go past 32 rounds.
ch04.s10.c3: It learns from a settled label: stop once no later round would have been right. It is built, but never run.
ch04.s11.c1: A block is one look, compare and think unit, built from attention and a small network.
ch04.s11.c2: Guess how many learned numbers in a block, where each vector is 512 numbers wide? About 4.62 million.
ch04.s11.c3: By our arithmetic, 21 blocks alone give 97.1 million. An older plan said 30 blocks, about 139 million.
ch04.s12.c1: The learned part comes in four sizes, named 3M, 10M, 30M and 100M for their rough size.
ch04.s12.c2: These are counts from the build. The finished design, B3, has not been run at any of these sizes yet.
ch04.s12.c3: As built, without the planned talker, the whole model at the 100 million step is 373.1 million numbers, borrowed reader included.
ch04.s13.c1: Is it cheaper if every letter talks to every letter? An average question has 81 letters. That is 81 times 81, or 6,561 checks.
ch04.s13.c2: Notes look at letters instead. A rough count: 44 notes, each looking at 81 letters and 27 number slots, is 4,752 checks a round.
ch04.s13.c3: Over 8 rounds, the older count, that is 4,752 times 8, or 38,016. At 81 letters, no work is saved.
ch04.s13.c4: Its gain is structure, not speed. By this count, much longer text would favour the notes, but that is untested.
ch04.s14.c1: Now a first result. In the first completed test, on an older design, one copy at the smallest size scored 73.01 points out of 100, thinking on, on 6,040 kept-aside questions.
ch04.s14.c2: Switch the thinking off, zero rounds, and the same copy scored 0.66 points.
ch04.s14.c3: One copy, one size. Hold that thought: Part 8 explains the test and its checks.
ch04.s15.c1: Not known: the thinker has never been tested at 100 million numbers.
ch04.s15.c2: Not known: whether many rounds hurt. One older probe, on one seed, found 16 rounds cost 1.2 to 1.9 points.
ch04.s15.c3: Experts, many small specialist networks, are a separate idea, not yet tested and not covered here.
ch04.s15.c4: Remember: it looks, passes notes and thinks, in rounds. The bell is built, not tested. But how does it use an outside calculator? Find out next.
